Momentous 61st Venice Biennale Ends With 2nd-Highest Visitor Turnout

Political disputes, a historic strike, and the curator's sudden passing did not keep visitors away.

The 61st Venice Biennale, curated by the late Koyo Kouoh, concluded yesterday, November 22, reporting 714,015 visitors during its six-month run. Nearly 30,000 visitors attended the pre-opening of In Minor Keys, which included a record-high 100 participating countries.

Despite running three weeks shorter than previous editions to allow for the installation of the renovated Central Pavilion at the Giardini, In Minor Keys is the second highest-attended exhibition in the event's history. (The 2022 edition holds the record, counting more than 800,000 visitors.) The news follows the highest-ever visitor numbers at the most recent editions of the Venice Architecture Biennale and Venice International Film Festival, two other landmark events organized under the La Biennale di Venezia.

Following Kouoh's unprecedented death in May 2025 at the age of 57, her team of collaborators — Rasha Salti, Marie Hélène Pereira, Gabe Beckhurst Feijoo, Siddhartha Mitter, and Rory Tsapayi — carried out the exhibition of 109 international artists, many of whom hailed from Africa and the Caribbean diasporas.

Hank Willis Thomas’s Sleight of Hand

The artist makes us supremely conscious of being spectators in a society that streams out images faster than factories churn out products.

Hank Willis Thomas has the rare ability to turn the everyday into a spark, all informed by a mashup of ad-man and bro aesthetics that flips through magazines, dabbles in sports, and repurposes the trappings of nationhood and masculinity. In a seemingly effortless way, he makes us supremely conscious of being spectators in a society that streams out images faster than factories churn out products.

His skill excites us with the idea that art can communicate to the rest of the world an inner reality negotiated through medium, history, and word play. Sometimes those elements feel meme-like, harvesting popular discourse in a way that frames it for more rarefied spaces like the art museum — his playfulness with All Lives Matter is a prime example. Other times he’s tapping historical veins for conceptual moments he can elevate or criticize with a little tweak, like the I Am a Man series (2012) that riffs on the Civil Rights protest sign.

For Some Artists, Residency-Hopping Is a Form of Survival

Artists are increasingly turning to the programs as sites of refuge as they navigate precarity, commercial pressures, and burnout.

For Paul Maheke, a French-born performance artist in his 40s, a year of funding, a sunlit studio in a sixteenth-century palatial estate in Rome, and ample time alone represented a new phase in a career that has long been shaped by transience. Over the last decade, before landing at the Villa Medici, he’d completed more than 14 artist residencies.

By 2015, after graduate school, he began moving between residencies every few months, relocating to remote locations in France, Vienna, and Canada. He sought distance from London’s commercial gallery circuit, a networking scene he described as populated with “opening-rats” and an environment he felt was depleting his focus. “Residencies were a way around that,” he told Hyperallergic, four months into his stay at the Italian complex. “I think I’ve never been sedentary. I tend to think better when I’m in movement. As I’m traveling, it’s always shifting my way of working.”

As his ideas developed, Maheke said that the pressure to hold down a studio space better suited to a painter no longer made sense. His work had outgrown a conventional studio, encompassing choreographed performances with professional dancers and drawing on autobiography. He described enmeshing an “Afro-descendant European perspective” with ideas about queerness, memory, and the body as a vessel for social experience.

Across countries and career stages, artists like Maheke have found themselves increasingly turning to residencies to navigate precarity. In interviews with Hyperallergic, artists reported using residencies as alternatives for permanent studios and refuges from the commercial pressures of major cultural centers. What were once considered philanthropic sites for creative retreat or intellectual leisure have become for many a workaround for periods of economic volatility and increased pressure to sustain artistic output.

Orthodox Cleric Wanted in Connection With International Forgery Scheme

Greek police has arrested one man in the $1.85 million art trafficking case.

A 44-year-old man was arrested during an undercover operation into an art forgery scheme in Athens, Greece, on Saturday, November 21, exposing an international network allegedly overseen by a Florida-based Orthodox priest. The arrest subsequently yielded the discovery of 35 forged paintings falsely attributed to prominent Greek and international artists, among other valuables.

The man, who remains unidentified to the public, was arrested on his way to make a sale to an undercover cop who posed as a client online. He had six paintings that he was going to sell to the undercover agents for €5,150 ($5,613). The investigation began in early October, when an art specialist tipped off authorities after encountering an online listing of two paintings attributed to famous 20th-century Greek expressionist George Bouzianis with counterfeit certificates of authenticity for sale.

Joni Mitchell Has Some News

In a collection of political paintings, the famed musician and artist lambastes MAGA, the Epstein class, and Trump's attacks on immigrants.

In her song “A Case of You,” Joni Mitchell described herself as “a lonely painter / I live in a box of paints.” She has never been a particularly shy one. The famously elusive artist, who has pronounced painting her "first love" before music, makes plain statements in NEWS, a collection of political paintings.

Conceived and designed by Mitchell, the book unfurls a scathing rebuke of recent Republican administrations in the United States. Twenty-three paintings are presented chronologically, with a handful created between 2001 and 2004 and the majority made in the last 18 months. Works from the Bush years show the Twin Towers aflame with a sinister face in the smoke or a bare-chested blonde woman who sits astride Osama Bin Laden’s shoulders.

More recent works feature Adolf Hitler with the letters "MGGA" ("Make Germany Great Again"), former DHS Secretary Kristi Noem on horseback labeled “grifter,” and a triptych of Jeffrey Epstein, Ghislaine Maxwell, and President Trump as disgraced royalty playing cards. A spread of all the works becomes a Thunderdome-like arena of modern US politics — ending with a self-portrait of Mitchell receiving a Kennedy Center Honor. As if the answer to all that chaos is elevating impactful art.

Trump Staffer Unwittingly Reveals Smithsonian Takeover Plan

Reviews of the institution's exhibitions, termination of the American History Museum director, and financial restructuring are all on the line.

With no sign of ceasing its attacks on the Smithsonian Institution, the White House could further upend the museum and research network, according to a supposed Trump staffer's documents for a tentative overhaul strategy, which were photographed on a Metro train in Washington, DC.

The photos, which a commuter took and dispatched to ProPublica, outline 25 items under the "Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan," including the firing of National Museum of American History (NMAH) director Anthea Hartig, planned exhibitions on American nationalism, a redesigned logo and brand, and new institution-wide guidelines. If implemented, the measures could give the White House unparalleled authority over the Smithsonian's operations.

While the identity of the staffer has not been confirmed, ProPublica's report from today, November 23, speculates that it was Sam Bock, an associate policy adviser for the Trump-appointed Domestic Policy Council, which produced a draconian 162-page report in July that accused museum leadership, including Hartig, of promoting “extreme political activism."

Why it is here: original reporting, evidence and concrete detail

Inside Edward Said’s World

A new film about the Palestinian thinker, reviewed by a former students of his, and when does a documentary become an art performance?

‘Tis the season for great documentaries. Twenty years after the death of Palestinian literary critic and theorist Edward Said, a new film revisits his life and legacy. Moustafa Bayoumi, a student of Said himself, posits that it offers a new generation a glimpse of Said’s indomitable energy and inexhaustible fight.

The lovely Eileen G’Sell takes a look at Trisha Ziff’s latest documentary, Frida: The Girl That Just Doesn’t Go Away, which screened recently at DOC NYC. The film considers the commercial afterlife of Frida Kahlo, asking how the artist’s personal history has been whitewashed even as her image circulates endlessly through retail culture. What happens when an artist’s legacy becomes as much a consumer product as a creative one?

And finally, if you haven’t seen Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything, what are you waiting for? It may be the best film I’ve seen all year, full of unexpected twists, turns, and glorious awkward pauses. Though billed as a documentary, the film raises what I think is a more intriguing question: Is Fielder a performance artist playing a documentarian? Not to toot my own horn, but I explore that possibility and more in my recent review, though be warned: spoilers abound.

—Rebecca Schiffman, associate editor

Nathan Fielder Is a Performance Artist in Disguise

As an art historian, it’s hard not to relate what you see in everyday life to history — not in the sense that every lily pad recalls Monet or snowballs bring David Hammons to mind, but in the sense that sometimes art really does imitate life. This happened to me recently, maybe 10 minutes into Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s You Can See Everything. I watched Fielder hold painful, prolonged eye contact with Elizabeth Holmes, the convicted fraudster whose eerily large blue eyes seem to enact their own kind of performance. Naturally, I thought of Marina Abramović’s “The Artist is Present” (2010). Perhaps it’s an obvious, pretentious comparison. But hear me out: Is Fielder a documentarian, or is he a performance artist playing one? | Rebecca Schiffman

Su Blackwell Enchants with Folkloric Stories That Spring from Vintage Books

From vintage tomes and encyclopedic volumes, British artist Su Blackwell carves, slices, and reconfigures text-laden pages into enchanting sculptures. Her latest body of work, opening this week in a solo show titled Pathway of Crumbs, draws on fairytales and folklore, a fitting topic for such dreamlike scenes.

Nodding to the enduring children’s story of Hansel and Gretel, the exhibition roots in nature and the stories we draw from the world around us. “In Flight,” for example, stretches nearly 3.5 feet as a swarm of butterflies emerges from the flared pages of a book. “Break off my Branches” is similarly dynamic, with a flock of multi-colored birds perched on the spindly stems that burst from a splayed edition.

Blackwell selected this particular set of books because they’ve been in her collection for several years, allowing the artist to digest their contents and ruminate on how they might emerge over time. Some she’s left in the same condition since purchasing them from a secondhand shop, and others she’s minimally cut and spliced for earlier projects. All, though, have remained a compelling artifact of human knowledge and a collective desire to create, one she transforms anew into striking compositions at the intersection of nature and culture.

Pathway of Crumbs is on view from November 25 to January 25 at Long & Ryle in London. Find more from Blackwell on her website.
